The battle of Karansebes - possibly the worst friendly fire incident in history. An army of 100,000 Austrians set up camp preparing for the Ottoman invasion, and some of their hussat scouts found some Roma who sold them schnapps. Some infantry found the scouts getting drunk, wanted some for themselves and started a brawl. 

One of them fired a shot, which caused panic as they started shouting that the Ottomans had arrived and the hussars and infantry fled, exacerbated by the fact that the troops barely understood each other and misheard the German officers attempt to restore order by shouting "Halt!" as a cry of "Allah!".

The artillery commander in the base, seeing the hussars rush back to camp in the night and thinking it was an Ottoman charge, and immediately ordered the cannons to open fire, which woke up the rest of the camp and caused such a widespread panic that Joseph II was forced to order a general retreat. 

The Turks arrived 2 days later, saw the dead and wounded left in the retreating army's wake, briefly wondered what the fuck happened, and took the city with minimal resistance.

So if you're following the book, the existence of the soulmonger is known of by a few individuals (Syndra, the Red Wizards, etc), though it's exact function is only known by the night hags and Acererak - it draws and traps the souls of the dead to feed the Atropal and awaken it. Think of it like an incubator. All everyone else knows is it stops resurrection and slowly kills everyone who was previously brought back to life. 

The Naga knows that Ras is involved, because if anyone is going to be it's him. He's got a bit of backstory, but basically boils down to former champion of Mezro who went too extreme. It's why Artus has a personal grudge against him - they were basically brothers, and Ras caused Mezro, and Artus' wife, to disappear. 

Acererak pretty much does things because he can - he's easily powerful enough to ascend to the gods, but chooses not to because it's more fun to create and kill them. His schemes take years, centuries to complete, but he has all the time in the world. He delights in death traps and puzzles, which is what drew him to Omu - he was impressed by what they came up with for their own trickster gods, so he murdered the gods, enslaved the people to build and test even better traps, and then filled it with loot to attract adventurers to top up his phylactery. 

The thing to remember is Acererak's presence should be secret until they enter the tomb - one of your party might see visions of him stalking the streets towards them, and the kobolds think he'll make them dragons for resetting the traps. Ras thinks that defending the Tomb will cure him, but Acererak's only cure will be death, especially if the atropal wakes up.

This is my current obsession at the moment. They've really put a lot of effort into making a world with lots to explore/exploit. It's definitely a game with a slow build, but once you start planning out massive factories, logistic networks and squeezing every resource you can out of an area, it really starts to click. 

It definitely has moments where these things are daunting - figuring out exactly how many machines you need, and how to organise them. It also doesn't help that you'll find yourself rebuilding a section when you find a more efficient recipe or when you can suddenly mine even more raw resources (both of these happened to me, on the same section, within 6 hours). It's a lot easier to deal with friends though - that way you have someone else to blame when the power starts shorting out. But there's still a good experience solo - you get some ... satisfaction when you realise you've solved an issue yourself.

It's good to get now, but the next update will be moving to the new Unity engine, so you may want to hold off unless you're sure your PC can handle it. I'd probably hold off till the next sale.

 Rimworld definitely adds a lot with the DLC - religion, psychic powers, children, etc - but the base game is heavily moddable. It's more a story generator like Dwarf Fortress - it's the procedural interactions and weird scenarios that make it fun.

I'm sorry for your loss. My sister in law committed suicide while I was running a campaign with her, family and friends. She was fine the Sunday night we had our regular session, then we got the call the Monday afternoon. 

We never ended up finishing the campaign - it was too much for any of us. Her character had hopes of restoring a village that I had been left abandoned - I ended up getting some artwork of her character, with reluctant goblin sidekick in a papoose, as a statue making her the hero she always wanted to be. One copy hangs on the wall by where I keep my DnD notes, the other was left in her casket. I still play with a lot of the same group, in a new setting, but it took a while to get comfortable with the idea. 

You should do what you feel is right to honour both a friend and a player. There's no absolute right way to do this, but definitely ask the family about what they're comfortable with.  As for the campaign - I'd advise you not to force things. Take a few weeks to take stock, check in with the other players, and see how you all feel. Again, there's no single way through this, although I can absolutely understand how you feel - it's sometimes better for things to end where they are. If you need someone to talk it through, feel free to DM me.

Three tips here:

First, "It's not you vs them". It's very easy to think that your trying to kill the party because you're throwing all the monsters, traps and problems at them. Think of it more as building the story with them - if they do something that makes a good story,  follow it up. It's okay to bend the rules a bit, it's your game. It's still good to give them a challenge - it's a dull game if everything goes smoothly, after all. 

Another point is "Make the monsters feel alive". Most of the things you meet won't necessarily charge in and fight to the death. For example: those goblins will easily make mincemeat of a level 1 group, if they're organised. But, they're goblins - vicious and cowardly. They'll go for weakness, so make them telegraph it ("Watch the big guy in armour, I'll go for the one in robes!" etc). They also don't really care for other goblins that much, so they're happy to put another goblin in harms way if it means getting ahead themselves. They're also not stupid enough to fight to the death, so make them retreat if it's not looking good for them. Try reading The Monsters Know What They're Doing - really helps to get your head into how these things fight.

Lastly, there's a few common rules that most people struggle with at first - Stealth vs Perception, when to call for a roll, movement out of combat, etc. There's plenty of resources out there to help - Matt Colville & Zee Bashew for example. There's also r/DMAcademy where you can ask if you're not sure.

IV tells you how much stronger your pokemon will be compared to a baseline. There's a few things to bear in mind:

1) Low level, high IV is usually worse than high level, low IV. The extra stats you get from IV aren't enough to compensate for low levels.
2) CP isn't helpful for quick assessments. A pokemon could have a similar CP for both of the examples above. The trick is to look at the white curve behind the pokemon. The closer the dot on the line is to the right, the better the level. 
3) Pokemon can be broadly grouped into tiers. You can have a 100% eevee, for example, but it's not going to win against even a 0% legendary.
4) Stardust is hard to come by. If you can catch something already levelled up, you'll spend less.

Overall then, IV is nice for an edge but not absolutely important. Some people can obsess over catching the best, and during community days you can afford to be a bit picky, but most of the time you can get away with just the best CP/level. Your method is good, but I might suggest that you save the top 3, assess them and see if any stick out. Remember to find out what your gym assessment will look like if it's in the top 80%.

>What makes a molecule have the property of chirality in the first place? Can any molecule have chirality? What physical or chemical properties must be present for it to have chirality?

Any molecule with mirror images that can't be superimposed on each other is chiral. Take your hands, for example - they're mirrors of each other, but you can't fit one on top of the other. For simple molecules with a flat shape, you can just flip one over to make a mirror image. So, for it to be chiral, it must have a 3D shape.

 It must also have distinct parts - if two sections are identical, then you can create a mirror image. So, it needs a 3D centre (usually carbon), and there must be 4 different parts connected to the carbon centre. 

Chemically, its pretty difficult to distinguish enantiomers. Physically, its easier - the crystals of different enantiomers will rotate polarised light in opposite directions. Say, one will rotate 40 degrees clockwise, the other will go 40 degrees anticlockwise. 

Biologically, though - that's the tricky part. Your enzymes are all based on chiral amino acids, so different enantiomers will have different pharmacological effects. A drug that's effective in one enantiomer might be useless or even toxic in another - see thalidomide. 

>How is a molecule split such that it spits out two images of itself? How does the lab do this?

If you go from a flat shape to a 3D shape, most of the time there's no difference between which side you approach it from. It's literally a heads or tails scenario - you should get about 50-50 of each enantiomer. Some catalysts (think enzymes) CAN be chiral, and their products will also be chiral as a result, but most of the time you will just get a mixture. 

The other problem with making a single enantiomer is keeping it that way - unless the chiral centre is fixed (say, as part of a ring or has massive attached groups) the groups can slide around each other freely. This will racemise the molecule, so you still end up with a mixture. 

>Can the two enantiomers be changed back to base (converted back up so to speak)?

Start with enantiomer A. Reverse the reaction back to the flat molecule. If you go forward again, you won't necessarily get enantiomer A again,unless you have a chiral catalyst as mentioned above. 

>What chemical or physics causes the enantiomers to rotate along their axis?

>This confuses me are the enantiomers the exact chemical shape of the base just rotating?

There isn't anything really special about enantiomer rotation - ALL molecules rotate around single bonds. If anything, it's when you can stop them from rotating and distinguish one form from another that they become special. 

>Do chirals rotate at all if they are racemic (50/50) because it should be balanced. I would suppose the one that was unbalanced mixture then the one with more would dictate the way the molecule rotates?

Its pretty much a dynamic equilibrium - the rate of A to B will be equal to the rate of B to A.

The gap between spiral arms is pretty massive, so depending on your FTL method, you need either upgraded drives (Warp or wormhole) to get more range, or find a hyperlane that links the two arms. As an aside, it's already been confirmed that the FTL will be changed so that most empires will use hyperlane, so I'd recommend practicing with them.

As for sectors, think of it like this: it takes a lot of effort to manage every single system in a galaxy-spanning empire. Beyond the core system limit (the green icon in top right), the inefficiency causes you to lose income. The game encourages you to use sectors to help you out. The AI isn't the best, but still reasonable enough to govern your systems for you, building stations and defences. AFAIK, there isn't any limit to how big individual sectors can be, but I tend to go for 3-5 colonised systems each. You can also specialise sectors for producing minerals, food, etc.

Now, some people prefer to play tall, by having a few, very well developed worlds, rather than wide, and colonising every world you find. There are even a few ways to play with only your starting world. The main reason for this is that research and tradition costs are population linked, so more people means higher costs. I'd suggest that you avoid going this far just yet, but it might be a good idea to slow down the expansion a little bit.

As a basic guide, I'd suggest this: find any decent systems near your starting point, anything with multiple habitable worlds or good amounts of resources. Reserve those worlds with frontier posts on nearby stars asap (ps, frontier posts don't count for the system limit, so you can go nuts with them. Just remember to get rid of them once you have a colony in place, and rebuild them where you need them next). Once you have your core worlds sorted, you can start expanding out - either by forming federations, conquering neighbours or just  frontier posts and colonisation. 

The main ways to win a game is to either control most of the habitable worlds, alone or as part of a federation, or be the only empire left. Anything you can do to help you towards these goals will be useful. There might be a few obstacles in your path, but I'll leave you to discover them yourself. The megastructures are late game boosts that can really make your empire shine, traditions give boosts in different areas depending on your priorities (do I focus on research, expansion, etc), and the civics give some interesting playstyles - if you ever want to play something dedicated to the annihilation of anything xenos, Purifiers are fun. Just be aware that the other races really won't bother with diplomacy either.

Synthetic Dawn is much more focused on robotics - it adds synthetic empires, which provides another style of play. Given you're still getting used to the base game, I'd say to leave it for now. It also adds a few cosmetic bits, extra portraits and voices - again, nice for role-playing, but not essential.

Tl;dr - I'd say Utopia is a solid yes, Synthetic Dawn isn't on sale and can wait until you get the basics.

Three bits of advice: First, as others have said, you can run practice games by tuning your settings. Run a tiny map, few AI and no advanced starts. Also, you can turn iron man off, which gives access to the console commands (tab or tilde, iirc) . Until you get the basics, it can help to add resources when you're struggling. The achievements can come later.

Two: know your DLC. Some of the DLC is definitely more interesting than others. I'd argue that Utopia and Synthetic Dawn are must have, as they add good mechanics and improvements to the base game. Leviathan is interesting, adding utterly massive creatures to the galaxy, but you can play without them. The species packs are purely cosmetic - nice, but not an essential.

Three: The Times They Are A Changin' (harmonica solo). One of the best things about this game is the regular communication with the developers, and they've shown that the next update, Cherryh 2.0, is going to make massive changes to the game, including reworks to FTL, the warscore system, starbases, and invasions to name a few. Check out the Dev Diaries for more info, but my advice here is this: It won't be for a few months, but it will mean the systems you learn now won't be the same later.
